# The cast

<!-- Generated by scripts/export-cast.mjs — run `npm run cast`. Do not edit. -->

Almost nobody in this game is written. The Chief of Staff is, and the rest
are drawn from the run's seed out of the pools below — which means a cast
list is really a list of *what can be drawn*, plus the handful of people
who are always the same.

## The one fixed person

**Ruth Ellery** — Chief of Staff. Competence 91, loyalty 88, moderate,
temperament `institutionalist`. She is the only member of the cabinet whose
numbers do not move with the seed, because she is the voice that teaches the
job and a teacher who changes every run teaches nothing. Her lines live in
`src/game/chief.ts` rather than being drawn from a temperament.

## The offices

Six seats. The Chief of Staff is fixed; the other five are drawn fresh each
run, and each one's domain is what their competence actually improves.

| Office | Title | Domain |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `chief` | Chief of Staff | `politics` |
| `treasury` | Treasury Secretary | `economy` |
| `state` | Secretary of State | `foreign` |
| `defense` | Defense Secretary | `security` |
| `justice` | Attorney General | `justice` |
| `health` | Health Secretary | `health` |

## Temperaments

Why a secretary is in the room — the third thing, after competence and
loyalty. It decides what erodes them, what they bring to a crisis in their
lane, and whether the day they stop believing in you ends with a resignation
letter or a reporter's phone number.

There are 6 temperaments and five seats, dealt without replacement, so
every run seats five distinct ones and leaves a different one out. Who is
missing is part of the cast.

| Temperament | Who they are |
| --- | --- |
| **a true believer** `believer` | Came for the agenda, not the job. Reads every compromise as a retreat. |
| **an operator** `operator` | Was somebody before this and intends to be somebody after. Counts the room. |
| **an institutionalist** `institutionalist` | Thirty years in the building. Serves the office, and is not confused about which one. |
| **a rival** `rival` | Wanted this desk, nearly got it, and took the department instead. |
| **an old friend** `friend` | Knew you before the motorcade. Tells you the truth and takes the hit for it. |
| **a technocrat** `technocrat` | Here for the work. Your approval rating is weather, and they brought a coat. |

### What wears them down

Multipliers on the cabinet's base erosion, not absolute rates — each column
averages about 1, so the overall turnover rate is unchanged and what varies
is *which* of them goes and *why*. `Floor` is the loyalty ordinary
unpopularity cannot take them below; scandal and unrest go straight through
it. `Edge` is added to their competence on a crisis in their own department.

| Temperament | Drift | Approval | Scandal | Unrest | Floor | Leaks | Edge |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `believer` | 0.9 | 0.6 | 1.3 | 0.8 | 22 | 20% | 0 |
| `operator` | 1.25 | 1.8 | 1.2 | 0.9 | 0 | 78% | -5 |
| `institutionalist` | 0.75 | 0.2 | 2 | 0.7 | 30 | 10% | +7 |
| `rival` | 1.35 | 1.6 | 0.9 | 1.1 | 0 | 70% | +4 |
| `friend` | 0.7 | 0.4 | 0.7 | 0.7 | 34 | 0% | -3 |
| `technocrat` | 0.85 | 0.3 | 0.8 | 2.2 | 26 | 28% | +9 |

### What they say

**a true believer** `believer`

- *loyal* — says the thing you are all avoiding, and says it first
- *loyal* — has rewritten the proposal overnight, again, and it is better
- *sour* — has stopped arguing with you, which is worse than when they did
- *sour* — asks, carefully, what the plan was supposed to have been
- *parting* — leaves saying the administration lost its nerve, and is quoted saying it

**an operator** `operator`

- *loyal* — agrees with whatever the room has decided, a half-second after it decides
- *loyal* — has already told three reporters this was your idea
- *sour* — is taking meetings that are not on the schedule
- *sour* — has begun saying “the President's decision” where they used to say “we”
- *parting* — resigns to spend time with a family nobody has met, and takes the file with them

**an institutionalist** `institutionalist`

- *loyal* — notes, without emphasis, that this has been tried twice before
- *loyal* — has the precedent, the memo and the date it went wrong
- *sour* — has started putting things in writing
- *sour* — asks for the instruction in a signed document, which is not a question
- *parting* — resigns on principle, in a letter the whole country reads

**a rival** `rival`

- *loyal* — disagrees with you fluently, in front of people, and is often right
- *loyal* — runs their department like a campaign, because it is one
- *sour* — has a speech scheduled in a state that votes early
- *sour* — praised you this morning in a way that will be clipped
- *parting* — resigns without warning, and books the Sunday shows for the weekend

**an old friend** `friend`

- *loyal* — asks how you are, and waits for the real answer
- *loyal* — stays behind after the room empties, the way they always have
- *sour* — looks tired in a way that is about this building rather than the hours
- *sour* — has stopped saying the thing they used to say to you in private
- *parting* — steps down quietly for health reasons, and means it

**a technocrat** `technocrat`

- *loyal* — has brought a chart nobody asked for and everybody needed
- *loyal* — answers the question that was asked, which startles the room
- *sour* — has stopped bringing the chart
- *sour* — gives you the number and no longer tells you what it means
- *parting* — returns to the university, and publishes within the year

## Where the names come from

Cabinet secretaries draw a first name from 24 and a surname from 20.
Both halves have to be unused, not just the full name: a cabinet holding a
Yusuf Nakamura, a Yusuf Osei and a Naomi Osei reads as a bug.

**First** — Margaret, Daniel, Ruth, Marcus, Eleanor, Priya, Thomas, Grace, Andre, Helen, Victor, Naomi, Charles, Rosa, Edward, Fiona, Malcolm, Diane, Samuel, Yusuf, Claire, Nathan, Imani, Walter.

**Surnames** — Halloran, Nakamura, Beaumont, Osei, Lindqvist, Marchetti, Whitfield, Okonkwo, Petrov, Calderon, Ashworth, Dubois, Ferreira, Kowalski, Sandoval, Brennan, Vasquez, Ellery, Rasmussen, Tanaka.

**Spouse first names** (14) — Elena, Marcus, Nadia, David, Priya, Jonah, Claire, Samuel, Rosa, Michael, Ines, Adam, Leah, Nicholas.

**Children's first names** (16) — Maya, Theo, Aisha, Danny, Nora, Elliot, Sofia, Caleb, Ruth, Jonah, Cleo, Isaac, Mara, Owen, Nell, Felix.

## The family

A spouse and two children, each with a life running whether you are in it or
not. `personal.marriage` and `personal.family` are read off these people the
way approval is read off the blocs: the scalar is a readout, not the model.

| Who | Age | Opening bond |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Spouse | your age −6 to +4 | 68–80 |
| Elder child | 20–29 | 62–78 |
| Younger child | 9 to (elder − 5) | 62–78 |

### What a spouse gave up

- a paediatric surgery practice, now down to one clinic a month
- a law school deanship, deferred until the term is over
- a novel that has been three chapters from finished for two years
- an architecture firm they still call into at seven every morning
- a career in public health they left the week you announced
- a restaurant they opened at thirty and handed to a manager at fifty

### What a child is doing

**7–12**

- third grade, and a school run that now involves two vehicles
- obsessed with astronomy and unimpressed by your job
- learning the cello badly and with total commitment
- the only kid at school whose friends get background checks

**13–17**

- eleventh grade, and furious about the security detail
- captain of a team you have seen play twice
- applying to colleges and refusing all help from you
- in a band that rehearses in a room with a Secret Service agent in it

**18–23**

- second year at a university that will not stop calling you
- on a gap year, somewhere with poor phone reception
- studying marine biology and living with three strangers
- working a bar job under their mother's surname

**24–32**

- a junior architect who has never once asked you for anything
- a nurse working nights, which is when you are free
- teaching in a district your budget just cut
- starting a company you have politely not offered to help with

| **not well** `child-health` | child | 7–32 | 0.8 | There is a specialist appointment on the calendar you have not asked about. |

## Who can be talking

A conversation beat names a *role*, not a person, and the role resolves
against the actual state when the beat is shown — so a meeting written once
still works after a reshuffle. `src/game/speaker.ts`.

| Role | Resolves to | Dress |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `chief`, `treasury`, `state`, `defense`, `justice`, `health` | whoever holds that office now | suit |
| `spouse` | the spouse in `state.family` | smart |
| `child` | the first child in `state.family` | casual |
| `press` | the written figure — not simulated | smart |
| `ally` | the written figure — not simulated | suit |
| `room`, `narrator` | nobody; no face is drawn | — |

### Every speaker written into a meeting

| Name | Role | Title | Mood | Appears in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ruth Ellery | `chief` | Chief of Staff | `guarded` | Meet your cabinet; Address the joint session |
| The Treasury Secretary | `treasury` | Treasury Secretary | `neutral` | Meet your cabinet; Run a cabinet meeting |
| The Defense Secretary | `defense` | Defense Secretary | `concerned` | Meet your cabinet |
| The room | `room` |  | — | Meet your cabinet; Run a cabinet meeting |
| The Attorney General | `justice` | Attorney General | `guarded` | Meet your cabinet; Run a cabinet meeting |
| The chamber | `room` |  | — | Address the joint session |
| The Chief of Staff | `chief` | Chief of Staff | `guarded` | Run a cabinet meeting |
| The correspondent | `press` | Political correspondent | `hostile` | Sit for a hostile interview |
| The Prime Minister | `ally` | Head of government | `concerned` | Call an ally |
| Your spouse | `spouse` | your spouse | `warm` | Family dinner, no staff |
| One of your children | `child` | your child | `concerned` | Family dinner, no staff |

Seven moods are drawable: `neutral`, `warm`, `concerned`, `hostile`,
`tired`, `amused`, `guarded`. A beat that sets none gets one inferred from
its own text.

## The groups

Not characters, but they are who is in the room when a bill is counted, and
a secretary's faction is drawn from the first list.

### Congressional factions

| Faction | Axis | Party | Backed by | Hawks? | What they are |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **The Progressive Caucus** `progressives` | -1 | blue | `activists` | no | Small, loud, and willing to sink your bill to make a point. |
| **The Liberal Bloc** `liberals` | -0.5 | blue | `labour` | no | The mainstream of the blue party. Reliable until they are not. |
| **The Moderates** `moderates` | 0 | swing | `suburban` | yes | Cross-party, cautious, and the reason anything passes at all. |
| **The Conservative Bloc** `conservatives` | 0.5 | red | `business` | yes | Business-minded, allergic to deficits, open to a deal on the right terms. |
| **The Hardliners** `hardliners` | 1 | red | `traditionalists` | yes | They did not come here to compromise and they will tell you so. |

| Bloc | Share | Volatility | Blue / red lean | What moves them |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Unions and working families** `labour` | 17% | 0.22 | +8 / -8 | Jobs, wages, welfare, and whose side you take in a strike. |
| **Business and finance** `business` | 13% | 0.3 | -7 / +7 | Growth, the tax rate, the debt, and predictability. |
| **Older voters** `seniors` | 19% | 0.16 | -3 / +3 | Healthcare, prices, and the sense that things are under control. |
| **Younger voters** `young` | 15% | 0.34 | +9 / -9 | Education, climate, and whether anything ever changes. |
| **Rural and small-town** `rural` | 14% | 0.18 | -9 / +9 | Security, energy, guns, and being noticed at all. |
| **Suburban moderates** `suburban` | 16% | 0.28 | +1 / +1 | Schools, crime, competence, and the absence of drama. |
| **The activist left** `activists` | 3% | 0.42 | +14 / -16 | Climate, healthcare, and whether you fought or compromised. |
| **The traditionalist right** `traditionalists` | 3% | 0.42 | -16 / +14 | Defense, order, low taxes, and holding the line. |
